James O’Keefe on Felony Charges for Exposing Fraud in Minnesota:
Minnesota charged both myself and fellow journalist Cam Higby with two felony counts in
retaliation for our bombshell investigative report on voter vouching laws that we did back in
August.
We stand by our reporting.
The charges are an attempt to criminalize investigative journalism. The charges are an attempt
to distract from what our reporting exposed as insecure elections in Minnesota. Now, this has
become a landmark 1st Amendment case where everyone’s right to speak truth to power has
just been put on the line.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty led a press conference regarding these charges.
“Today we are charging two individuals, James O'Keefe and Cameron Higby, with felony counts
of unlawful voting and identity theft,” Moriarty said.
She also said that Cam and I could do some local jail time for our investigative reporting.
We received a charging document that lists two felony counts.
Count I: Identity Theft – knowingly misrepresented his identity in applying for a voting ballot
Count II: Unlawful Voting – knowingly misrepresented his identity in applying for a voting ballot
Two counts with the exact same justification beneath each count.
In our report, we clearly stopped and walked out of the polling places to avoid even touching a
voting ballot.
Moriarty even said it herself. She admitted that my and Higby’s intent was to act as investigative
reporters.
“A group of people were attempting to cast doubt on the state’s vouching system,” Moriarty
said. “I think it’s pretty clear they did not intend to vote.”
Moriarty also said there is no such thing as undercover journalism when looking into election
loopholes.
“If you identify as a journalist, there is no such thing as undercover investigation in the polling
place,” Moriarty said. “You have to identify yourself as a journalist in the polling place, which
they did not.”
Moriarty is wrong as a matter of constitutional law. The 1st Amendment allows reporters to
show up on Election Day and ask questions at polling booths.
But don’t take my word for it. In 2012, former Attorney General of the United States Eric Holder
went under oath in Washington, D.C. discussing an almost identical investigation asking if the
polling official has Eric Holder’s ballot at a precinct on primary day there.
“What I drew from that video was that [O’Keefe] was very careful not to say that he was Eric
Holder, not to actually get a ballot. He didn’t do the kinds of things that would have subjected
him to criminal prosecution,” Holder said.
In today’s press conference, Moriarty points out this distinction, too.
“So, there’s a difference between intent to vote and intent to apply for a ballot,” Moriarty said.
“The application of a ballot is a multi-step process. I can’t anticipate what [O’Keefe and Higby’s]
defense is. I’m sure we’ll hear from them.”
Our defense is the shield of the 1st Amendment to hold government accountable to the people.
We didn’t apply for a ballot; we were there talking to election clerks, posing hypotheticals, and
getting answers so that Americans could know what was happening in the elections.
Many people in the United States did not even know about vouching for eight, and this
investigative report educated them.
By the way, we conducted training and specifically told each journalist never to sign an affidavit,
never to procure a ballot, never to even touch a ballot.
We even did exercises training the journalists to say “the name is” rather than “my name is.” We
were very intentional about what we were there to do, namely was to inform the public.
Moriarty admitted that we stopped short of signing any oath or carrying out any fraud.
“Both men stopped short of signing the oath we all sign before receiving our ballot,” Moriarty
said.
The reporters in the room questioned Moriarty on what exactly we’re being prosecuted for.
“Does that give them a way to say that we didn’t commit a crime because we didn’t take it all
the way?” and followed up with, “Can you explain why you think it’s still a crime?”

🔻 Exclusive | Iran is pursuing energy diplomacy dynamically, resolutely: Minister

📌 Moscow, IRNA – Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard says Iran’s energy diplomacy is advancing dynamically and with strong resolve, despite challenges stemming from the hostile actions of its adversaries.

Bovard, who traveled to Moscow to accompany President Masoud Pezeshkian at the 8th Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) and to attend the forum's 28th Ministerial Meeting, made the remarks in an interview with IRNA on Wednesday.
​
He highlighted the outcomes of bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral consultations held by the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the Moscow summits, noting the prospect of attracting new Russian investment.
​
Referring to Pezeshkian's meeting with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, at the Kremlin, as well as his own bilateral discussions with the Russian Energy Minister, Bovard described the interactions between the two sides as positive and constructive.
​
He expressed hope that Russian investment in Iran—particularly in the development of the oil and gas industries—will increase based on the negotiations and agreements reached in Moscow, adding that the two sides also agreed to resolve issues affecting bilateral projects.
​
Responding to a question regarding the understanding on the transit of Russian gas to Iran, the Acting Oil Minister stated that there were positive outcomes of a trilateral meeting with Russian and Azerbaijani ministers, as the sides promised cooperation.
​
He noted that technical assessments are currently underway to determine whether the initial phase of Russian gas transit to Iran would be possible using existing pipelines across the three countries.
​
On the meetings held on the sidelines of the GECF in Moscow, Bovard pointed to talks with the Energy Minister of Qatar and the Minister of Petroleum and Gas of Libya, a bilateral meeting with the Minister of Petroleum and Energy of Senegal, consultations with the Venezuelan Minister of Petroleum, and a meeting with the CEO of the Russian state-owned company Gazprom.
​
The 8th GECF Summit was held in Moscow on Tuesday, attended by heads of state and high-level representatives from member countries. President Pezeshkian addressed the summit, emphasizing that member states must expand their cooperation in the areas of energy governance and strategic management.
​
A day earlier, Bovard addressed the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the GECF and presented the country's proposals and engaged in numerous consultations on the sidelines of the summit.
​
The Gas Exporting Countries Forum consists of 12 main member states: Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Iran, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru, and Senegal serve as observer states.
